extracted.intended_audience: advanced math-olympiad students, USAMO participants and coaches, problem-solvers on AoPS
extracted.subtask_description: Writing concise, advanced solution notes for USAMO-style olympiad problems (problem statements, claims/lemmas, and proofs), aimed at fellow contest solvers rather than beginners. Emphasizes standard theorems, terse exposition, and occasional references to community/organizer sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer terse, advanced exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: These notes will tend to be a bit more advanced and terse than the “official” solutions from the organizers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a theorem or technique is not known to beginners but is still considered “standard”, prefer to use it rather than try to work around or conceal it. Focus on conveying the main ideas succinctly rather than expanding elementary details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard theory without beginner-level justification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theorem or technique is still considered 'standard', the author often uses it without further comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in geometry use directed angles without further comment; omit sentences like 'let R denote the set of real numbers.' Do not belabor routine background that the intended audience is assumed to know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure solutions with claims/lemmas and proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize proofs by isolating intermediate facts as 'Claim — ... Proof.' or explicit lemmas before completing the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This improves readability and modularity: prove key subclaims, then assemble them to conclude. Use lemma statements for recurring toolkit facts (e.g., behavior of coefficients, geometric subfacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: State problem and provide source/link
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the problem statement and where the problem is available online (e.g., AoPS URL or video link).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly note 'Available online at https://...' or link to video resources. Acknowledge that solutions are a mix of own work, organizers' solutions, and community contributions, while maintaining authorial writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide remarks and explain which details are inessential
rubrics_metrics.description: Add short 'Remark.' paragraphs to point out simplifications, highlight that some technical details are unimportant, or note stronger/analogous statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use remarks to show where an assumption could be replaced, to point out historical occurrences of a claim, or to suggest alternative viewpoints (e.g., special-case intuition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer multiple proofs when illuminating
rubrics_metrics.description: When a lemma admits multiple natural proofs (e.g., Rolle's theorem vs Descartes' rule of signs), present more than one approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting alternative proofs shows different techniques and can aid readers with varied backgrounds; include brief sketches if full details are routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use WLOG reductions and standard simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, reduce generality early by selecting convenient subsets or assuming normalized parameters (e.g., taking n = k+1 WLOG).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the justification for the reduction succinctly; this keeps subsequent arguments clearer and avoids repetitive general-case bookkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present illustrative special cases before the general proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Give small or concrete examples (e.g., p = 5, n = p−1) to make patterns and modular/grouping arguments clear before proving the general statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples to motivate lemmas and to make the combinatorial/modular structure explicit; they serve as helpful intuition for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use constructive/algorithmic descriptions when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When the argument is inherently constructive (e.g., iterative deletion to obtain a perfect matching), describe the algorithm stepwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline the algorithm's steps, termination argument, and invariants. Show how the constructive procedure yields the desired distribution/assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoke standard heuristics and name common tools
rubrics_metrics.description: State common heuristics (e.g., 'for any compatible matching problem, Hall's condition is usually the go-to tool') and explicitly apply standard theorems (Chinese remainder theorem, Vieta formulas, Rolle's theorem, Descartes' rule of signs, Hall's marriage theorem, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these tools directly rather than re-proving them; remark when they are the natural heavy-lifting component of the solution and when an extra idea is needed alongside them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate problem-specific constructs to standard objects and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify known names for arising structures (e.g., the 'Bob-graph' is the Gabriel graph) and discuss connections or alternate constructions (e.g., relative neighbor graph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing out standard terminology helps situate the problem in existing literature and enables readers to leverage known properties of these objects (e.g., planar/connected properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures, cartoons, and diagrams to clarify geometry or combinatorial configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include sketches or cartoon diagrams for configurations that are clearer visually (e.g., showing disks with diameters, sequences of points, or arc partitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple labeled figures improve intuition for geometric arguments and for combinatorial/algorithmic manipulations; annotate key points, edges, and forbidden regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and use clear inductive/merging invariants in deletion arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying deletion-induction, make explicit how deletion affects other players' structures (e.g., merging arcs, preserving total value ≥1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the invariant that ensures induction works (e.g., merged arc value ≥1) and why endpoints/intersections behave as claimed so the induction step preserves hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage feedback and community corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly invite corrections and comments from readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State a willingness to accept corrections, and note when solutions combine community and organizer ideas; this supports collaborative improvement of notes.
